question: An internal agent for account managers can read CRM records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. Account managers only ever read records and draft emails through it. Under least privilege, what is the right change?

choices.A: Log every update and deletion for later audit
choices.B: Add a confirmation dialog before updates and deletions
choices.C: Restrict deletions to business hours
choices.D: Remove the update and delete capabilities from the agent's configuration entirely

explanation: **D.** Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, eliminating the attack and error surface rather than monitoring it. Logging (A) and confirmations (B) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and scheduling (C) narrows the window without closing it.

question: After a nightly document refresh, your RAG assistant's answers turned confident but wrong. Model version, prompts, and latency are unchanged. Where do you look first?

choices.A: The retrieval and indexing layer: whether the refresh broke the index, changed chunking, or introduced mismatched embeddings
choices.B: The model, which may have degraded overnight
choices.C: The system prompt wording
choices.D: The temperature setting

explanation: **A.** The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong is the signature of plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved context. The pinned model (B), unchanged prompt (C), and sampling (D) do not correlate with the refresh.

question: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities to agents across many teams. Loading all forty tool definitions into every agent's context is bloating prompts and degrading tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?

choices.A: Shorter tool descriptions across the board
choices.B: Progressive discovery: agents load a small task-relevant toolset, with search or namespacing to pull in others when needed
choices.C: One mega-tool with a mode parameter selecting among forty behaviors
choices.D: Limit the platform to ten capabilities

explanation: **B.** At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees what its task needs. Uniformly terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch mega-tool (C) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism entirely, and capping the platform (D) sacrifices the requirement.

question: A bank wants a system that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?

choices.A: The proposed multi-agent system, since both tasks involve documents
choices.B: One agent with all tools and a routing prompt
choices.C: Two simple components: a retrieval-augmented answer service for policy questions, and a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated on its own metrics
choices.D: A single fine-tuned model for both

explanation: **C.** Two well-understood problems with different shapes deserve the two cheapest reliable structures, independently testable and governable. Shared document-ness (A) is not an architectural argument, one agent with everything (B) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (D) is the most expensive path to problems retrieval and templates already solve.

question: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow over an autonomous agent for claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?

choices.A: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in general
choices.B: Workflows always outperform agents
choices.C: The team lacked time to build an agent
choices.D: The intake path is fully known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, auditable, and reliable; autonomy earns its complexity only where the model must choose the path

explanation: **D.** The framework is structural fit: known path, deterministic orchestration; open-ended path, agent. Novelty (A) and universal claims (B) are not engineering arguments, and resourcing (C) justifies a schedule, not an architecture.

question: Legal review quality is subjective, and your team disagrees about whether the assistant's clause summaries are "good." What makes evaluation tractable?

choices.A: Define a rubric with the failure modes that matter, build a labeled evaluation set with counsel, and combine rubric-based model grading with periodic human review
choices.B: Ship and count complaints
choices.C: Exact string match against one reference summary per clause
choices.D: Grade outputs by length

explanation: **A.** Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the judgment. Complaint-counting (B) measures too late, exact match (C) fails every valid paraphrase, and length (D) measures nothing.

question: A prompt change looks better in demos. Before rolling it to all users, what is the disciplined path?

choices.A: Roll it out; demos are representative
choices.B: Run it against the regression evaluation set, then A/B it against the current prompt on real traffic with predefined metrics before full rollout
choices.C: Ask the team to vote
choices.D: Roll out to everyone with a feedback banner

explanation: **B.** Changes to prompts are production changes: regression evaluation catches breakage, and an A/B on defined metrics establishes improvement before exposure. Demos (A) and votes (C) are anecdotes, and full rollout with a banner (D) is the experiment without the control.

question: A healthcare client requires that no protected health information reach the model provider, while clinicians want free-text queries about patients. Which design meets both?

choices.A: Trust clinicians to avoid typing identifiers
choices.B: A system prompt instructing the model to forget PHI
choices.C: A de-identification layer that strips or tokenizes PHI before the API call, re-associating results locally, with logging and periodic audits of the boundary
choices.D: Blocking free-text queries entirely

explanation: **C.** Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, and the control is auditable. Trust (A) is not a control, model instructions (B) act after the data already crossed, and a hard block (D) fails the stated business need that a compliant design can meet.

question: Your Claude solution's executive sponsor asks for "99.9% accuracy or we cancel." Accuracy on the task plateaus near 92% with human review catching the rest. What is the architect's correct move?

choices.A: Promise 99.9% and hope model upgrades close the gap
choices.B: Decline to discuss numbers with non-engineers
choices.C: Quietly redefine accuracy so the number reads higher
choices.D: Reframe the target around the end-to-end process: the system plus confidence-routed human review achieves the business outcome, with measured rates, costs, and the tradeoff curve made explicit

explanation: **D.** Managing expectations with explicit, honest tradeoffs is scored material at this level: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (A), stonewalling (B), and metric games (C) each destroy the trust the role exists to build.

question: Three teams configure Claude Code independently: conventions drift, and new engineers take days to become productive. What is the enablement fix?

choices.A: Ship a shared baseline: version-controlled team configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top
choices.B: Mandate that engineers memorize the conventions
choices.C: Prohibit Claude Code until conventions settle
choices.D: Let each engineer keep personal settings only

explanation: **A.** Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration with local extension, which is what makes tooling productive at organizational scale. Memorization (B) does not configure anything, prohibition (C) discards the productivity the domain exists to deliver, and personal-only settings (D) is the drift you started with.

question: A customer requires that no request data leave their AWS account. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?

choices.A: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement
choices.B: Claude through Amazon Bedrock within the customer's own account and region
choices.C: The Claude API with request logging disabled
choices.D: Any deployment, provided the data is encrypted in transit

explanation: **B.** A residency constraint of this kind is met by running within the customer's own cloud boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contractual agreement (A), disabled logging (C), and transport encryption (D) all still involve the data leaving the account.

question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit to run through existing controls. What follows?

choices.A: Deploy on Bedrock for feature parity
choices.B: Use the Claude API and replicate the controls
choices.C: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
choices.D: Let each team choose its own path

explanation: **C.** Aligning with the platform the enterprise already governs is what makes existing controls apply without duplication. A different cloud (A) creates a second control plane, replication (B) is expensive and drifts, and per-team choice (D) removes governance.

question: A design places Claude behind an internal service that every application calls. What is the principal benefit?

choices.A: It reduces token cost
choices.B: It removes the need for evaluation
choices.C: It guarantees lower latency
choices.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced in one place

explanation: **D.** A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not reduce token cost (A) or remove the need to evaluate (B), and an extra hop generally adds latency (C).

question: A legacy system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the task needs long reasoning. What is the appropriate design?

choices.A: Accept the request, return an identifier immediately, and deliver the result asynchronously
choices.B: Force the model to answer within two seconds
choices.C: Increase the legacy timeout
choices.D: Use the smallest model available

explanation: **A.** Decoupling submission from delivery lets the constraint and the workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating the reasoning (B, D) sacrifices the task, and changing the legacy system (C) is usually the constraint rather than an option.

question: What is the most important consideration when a solution must run across two clouds?

choices.A: Using identical prompts in both
choices.B: Establishing which behaviors must be identical and evaluating for those on each platform
choices.C: Choosing the cheaper platform for both
choices.D: Deploying to whichever region is nearest

explanation: **B.** Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified, not assumed. Identical prompts (A) do not guarantee identical behavior, and cost (C) and proximity (D) do not address consistency.

question: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous agent to handle an end-to-end financial approval process. What should the architect establish first?

choices.A: Which model to use
choices.B: The expected token cost
choices.C: Which decisions carry accountability and must remain with a person
choices.D: Whether the agent can be built in the available time

explanation: **C.** Where accountability sits determines the shape of the solution and what may be automated at all. Model choice (A), cost (B), and schedule (D) are all downstream of that boundary.

question: Two designs meet the functional requirement. One is simpler and slightly less capable. What should decide?

choices.A: The more capable design, since capability is the point
choices.B: The design the team finds more interesting
choices.C: The design with more components, for future flexibility
choices.D: Whether the extra capability is needed by a stated requirement, weighed against the cost of complexity

explanation: **D.** Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), preference (B), and speculative flexibility (C) all pay that cost without justification.

question: A proposed architecture depends on the model behaving correctly for a control that regulation requires. What is the correct judgment?

choices.A: Unacceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
choices.B: Acceptable if evaluation shows high accuracy
choices.C: Acceptable with a disclaimer to the regulator
choices.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

explanation: **A.** A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behavior cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. Accuracy (B), disclosure (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.

question: What is the clearest sign that a solution has been over-engineered?

choices.A: It uses more than one model
choices.B: Components exist that no stated requirement depends on
choices.C: It has an evaluation suite
choices.D: It includes a human approval step

explanation: **B.** Unjustified components are the definition of over-engineering and are the parts that will rot. Multiple models (A), evaluation (C), and approval steps (D) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.

question: What must exist before a solution can be said to be ready for production?

choices.A: A demonstration that impressed stakeholders
choices.B: Agreement from the engineering team
choices.C: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
choices.D: A completed cost estimate

explanation: **C.** Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what distinguishes it from an impression. Demonstrations (A), consensus (B), and cost (D) do not establish whether the system works.

question: An evaluation set is drawn entirely from cases the system already handles well. What is the consequence?

choices.A: It gives a reliable measure of quality
choices.B: It is acceptable if it is large enough
choices.C: It only matters for regulated systems
choices.D: It overstates performance and hides the failure modes that matter

explanation: **D.** An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and size cannot correct a biased sample. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix bias (B), and the problem is universal rather than sector-specific (C).

question: A prompt change improves the target metric but degrades an unmeasured behavior. How is this best prevented?

choices.A: Maintaining a regression suite that covers behaviors the system must not lose
choices.B: Changing one thing at a time
choices.C: Reviewing changes more carefully
choices.D: Limiting how often prompts change

explanation: **A.** Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break. Single changes (B) and careful review (C) reduce risk without detecting it, and slowing change (D) does not make it safe.

question: What should trigger re-evaluation of a deployed solution?

choices.A: Only a reported incident
choices.B: A change to the model, the prompt, the data distribution, or the requirement
choices.C: A fixed annual schedule
choices.D: A change in cost

explanation: **B.** Any change to the things that determine behavior invalidates prior measurement. Waiting for incidents (A) detects late, a fixed schedule (C) is unrelated to actual change, and cost (D) does not affect correctness.

question: How should an architect treat a request to log full prompts and responses for audit?

choices.A: Implement it, since audit requirements take precedence
choices.B: Refuse, since logging creates risk
choices.C: Establish what the audit actually requires, since prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
choices.D: Log responses only

explanation: **C.** Audit and data protection are both real constraints, and the design must satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket implementation (A) and blanket refusal (B) ignore one side, and a partial rule (D) is arbitrary without knowing the requirement.

question: What is the correct treatment of content retrieved from an untrusted source before it reaches the model?

choices.A: It is safe once scanned for known attack strings
choices.B: It is safe if the model is instructed to disregard instructions within it
choices.C: It is safe if it comes over an encrypted channel
choices.D: It is untrusted data throughout, and the model's authority must be bounded regardless of its content

explanation: **D.** The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its permissions whatever the content persuades it to attempt. String scanning (A) and prompt instructions (B) are bypassable, and transport security (C) says nothing about the content.

question: Who is accountable for a wrong decision produced by an automated Claude workflow?

choices.A: The organization that deployed the workflow
choices.B: The model provider
choices.C: The engineer who wrote the prompt
choices.D: Nobody, since the output was automated

explanation: **A.** Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (B) supplies a capability, individual authorship (C) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D).

question: An executive sponsor asks for a single number showing how good the solution is. What is the right response?

choices.A: Provide the headline accuracy figure
choices.B: Provide the measure that matches the decision they face, with its limits stated
choices.C: Explain that quality cannot be summarised
choices.D: Provide the model's benchmark score

explanation: **B.** A useful metric is one tied to the decision at hand and honest about what it does not cover. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark score (D) can mislead, and refusing to summarise (C) fails the sponsor.

question: A pilot succeeded with ten users and the business wants to roll out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?

choices.A: The cost of additional licenses
choices.B: The need for a larger model
choices.C: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
choices.D: The training schedule

explanation: **C.** Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming those is the architect's contribution. Licenses (A), model size (B), and training (D) are downstream of knowing what breaks.

question: What most reduces the risk that a delivered solution decays after handover?

choices.A: Full documentation at delivery
choices.B: A longer warranty period
choices.C: Training every user
choices.D: A named owner with a defined routine for evaluation, monitoring, and update

explanation: **D.** Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artefacts produced once. Documentation (A) and training (C) age, and a warranty (B) covers defects rather than drift.

question: How should an architect choose a model for a solution with several different tasks?

choices.A: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its requirement, and evaluate the choices
choices.B: One model for everything, for simplicity
choices.C: The largest model for everything, for safety
choices.D: The newest model for everything

explanation: **A.** Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit.

question: What is the correct treatment of the context window in a production design?

choices.A: A capacity to fill as fully as possible
choices.B: A budget to allocate deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
choices.C: A limit that only matters for long documents
choices.D: A setting to raise when quality drops

explanation: **B.** Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (A) invites dilution, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.

question: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged. What is the appropriate remedy?

choices.A: Appoint one team to own all prompting
choices.B: Freeze the prompts
choices.C: Version the prompts as artefacts with defined ownership, review, and evaluation on change
choices.D: Move all prompts into the system prompt

explanation: **C.** Prompts that determine production behavior deserve the same lifecycle as code. Centralising ownership (A) may not fit the organization, freezing (B) blocks improvement, and relocation (D) does not address governance.

question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across many repositories. What is the most durable approach?

choices.A: A written policy circulated by email
choices.B: A one-off training session
choices.C: Requiring approval for each use
choices.D: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code

explanation: **D.** Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (C) creates friction without conveying practice.

question: What is the most useful measure of whether a developer enablement program is working?

choices.A: Change in the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
choices.B: The number of people trained
choices.C: License utilization
choices.D: The volume of tool calls

explanation: **A.** Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, which is what should be measured. Attendance (B), utilization (C), and activity (D) measure uptake rather than benefit.

question: A team reports that Claude Code helps with new code but hurts on a legacy service. What should the architect investigate?

choices.A: Whether the team needs more training
choices.B: Whether the legacy service lacks the committed context and conventions the model needs
choices.C: Whether a larger model would help
choices.D: Whether the legacy service should be rewritten

explanation: **B.** A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each. Training (A) does not supply repository context, a larger model (C) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.

question: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalog that changes daily. Which architecture fits?

choices.A: Fine-tune a model on the catalog nightly
choices.B: Load the catalog into the system prompt
choices.C: Retrieval over an index refreshed as the catalog changes, with the model answering from retrieved context
choices.D: An autonomous agent that browses the public website

explanation: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window

question: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?

choices.A: The generation prompt
choices.B: The model version
choices.C: The user interface
choices.D: Chunking and embedding configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently

explanation: Degradation following a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency

question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?

choices.A: Scope toolsets per task or role, with progressive discovery for the rest
choices.B: Shorten all tool descriptions
choices.C: Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools
choices.D: Replace the agent with a larger model

explanation: At large tool counts, scoping and progressive discovery preserve selection quality

question: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?

choices.A: Exact match against reference summaries
choices.B: A rubric covering the failure modes that matter, applied by model graders and periodically audited by humans on a labeled set
choices.C: Average output length compared to references
choices.D: User thumbs-up counts alone

explanation: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology

question: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?

choices.A: Ship it and monitor complaints
choices.B: Team vote followed by rollout
choices.C: Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt on predefined metrics, then rollout
choices.D: Rollout with a feedback form

explanation: Prompt changes are production changes: regression first, then a controlled comparison

question: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?

choices.A: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
choices.B: A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI
choices.C: Restricting the feature to structured queries only
choices.D: A de-identification layer that removes or tokenizes PHI before the call, with local re-association and auditing

explanation: Compliance boundaries are enforced architecturally before data crosses, and audited

question: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?

choices.A: Route by confidence and consequence, so low-confidence and high-impact cases reach humans while routine cases flow through
choices.B: Review every output regardless of risk
choices.C: Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
choices.D: Review only what users complain about

explanation: Confidence and consequence routing makes human review affordable and effective

question: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?

choices.A: The highest observed number
choices.B: Performance broken out by document type with the aggregate, the measurement method, and what the business outcome is after human review
choices.C: A refusal to quantify
choices.D: An average weighted to look favorable

explanation: Honest segmentation plus method and end-to-end outcome is what earns and keeps trust

question: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?

choices.A: Response latency targets
choices.B: The choice of programming language
choices.C: Data minimization, purpose limitation, and the ability to delete personal data on request
choices.D: The number of model providers

explanation: GDPR drives minimization, purpose limitation, and erasure, all of which shape design

question: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?

choices.A: Workflows are always more accurate
choices.B: Agents cannot process documents
choices.C: Workflows use less context
choices.D: The processing path is known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable

explanation: Known path, deterministic orchestration; autonomy earns its complexity only when the path is not known

question: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?

choices.A: Ordering the static preamble first and enabling prompt caching
choices.B: Splitting the preamble across two requests
choices.C: Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
choices.D: Moving the preamble into a few-shot block

explanation: A stable cached prefix cuts time-to-first-token and per-request cost together

question: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?

choices.A: The final design only
choices.B: The decision, the alternatives considered, the tradeoffs, and the constraints that drove the choice
choices.C: The team members involved
choices.D: The implementation timeline

explanation: A decision record captures alternatives and tradeoffs, not just the outcome

question: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?

choices.A: Final outputs only
choices.B: Aggregate latency metrics only
choices.C: Traces of tool calls, retrieved context, and decision points alongside outputs
choices.D: User feedback only

explanation: Without traces of tool calls and retrieved context, failures cannot be localized to a layer

question: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?

choices.A: A recorded walkthrough
choices.B: A shared chat channel
choices.C: Individual coaching sessions
choices.D: Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path that new engineers follow

explanation: Shared, versioned configuration with an onboarding path is what makes adoption stick

question: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?

choices.A: Separating read and write capabilities, granting write access only where the role requires it, and gating writes behind explicit approval
choices.B: Logging modifications for later review
choices.C: Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
choices.D: Running the agent during business hours only

explanation: Least privilege plus approval gates on writes reduces the surface rather than monitoring it

question: A client requires that inference run inside their own AWS account. What does this determine?

choices.A: The model family only
choices.B: That a data processing agreement is sufficient
choices.C: Deployment through Amazon Bedrock in the client's account and region
choices.D: That request logging must be disabled

explanation: Running inside the client's own cloud boundary is what the requirement describes. A contract (B) and logging settings (D) do not keep the data in the account, and the model family (A) is a separate choice

question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud wants identity and audit handled by existing controls. What follows?

choices.A: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
choices.B: Use the Claude API and rebuild the controls
choices.C: Use Bedrock for feature parity
choices.D: Let each team decide

explanation: Aligning with the governed platform makes existing controls apply without duplication. Rebuilding (B) drifts, a different cloud (C) creates a second control plane, and per-team choice (D) removes governance

question: What is the main architectural benefit of routing all model traffic through one internal service?

choices.A: Lower token prices
choices.B: It removes the need for evaluation
choices.C: It guarantees lower latency
choices.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing are applied consistently in one place

explanation: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns are enforced and changed once. It does not change unit price (A), remove evaluation (B), or reduce latency (C)

question: Two designs both satisfy the requirement; one is materially simpler. What decides?

choices.A: The more capable design, since headroom is valuable
choices.B: Whether any stated requirement needs the extra capability, against the ongoing cost of complexity
choices.C: Whichever the team prefers to build
choices.D: The one with more components, for flexibility

explanation: Complexity is paid for continuously, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Headroom (A), preference (C), and speculative flexibility (D) pay that cost without justification

question: A required compliance control depends on the model behaving correctly. What is the correct judgment?

choices.A: Acceptable if measured accuracy is very high
choices.B: Not acceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
choices.C: Acceptable with a documented residual risk
choices.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

explanation: A control that must hold needs a guarantee, which probabilistic behavior cannot supply. High accuracy (A), documentation (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee

question: Where should the boundary of automation be drawn in a solution that makes customer-affecting decisions?

choices.A: Wherever the model performs well in testing
choices.B: As far as the budget allows
choices.C: At whatever the client requests
choices.D: Where accountability for the decision sits, keeping those decisions with a person

explanation: Accountability determines what may be automated at all, and that boundary is an architectural decision. Test performance (A), budget (B), and unexamined requests (C) do not address responsibility

question: What must exist before a solution is declared production-ready?

choices.A: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
choices.B: A successful demonstration
choices.C: Sign-off from the engineering team
choices.D: A completed cost model

explanation: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar. A demonstration (B), consensus (C), and cost (D) do not establish whether it works

question: An evaluation set contains only cases the system already handles. What is the effect?

choices.A: It provides a reliable quality measure
choices.B: It is fine if it is large
choices.C: It overstates performance and conceals the failures that matter
choices.D: It matters only in regulated contexts

explanation: An unrepresentative sample measures the wrong distribution, and size does not correct bias. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix it (B), and the problem is general (D)

question: How should a request to log every prompt and response for audit be handled?

choices.A: Implement it, since audit takes precedence
choices.B: Decline, because logging creates risk
choices.C: Log responses but not prompts
choices.D: Establish what the audit requires, because prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data

explanation: Audit and data protection are both real, and the design must serve the audit purpose without retaining more than warranted. Blanket action (A) or refusal (B) ignores one side, and an arbitrary split (C) is unjustified

question: Who is accountable when an automated Claude workflow produces a harmful decision?

choices.A: The model provider
choices.B: The engineer who wrote the prompt
choices.C: The organization that deployed it
choices.D: No one, because the decision was automated

explanation: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes. The provider (A) supplies a capability, individual authorship (B) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D)

question: A sponsor asks for one number that shows whether the solution is working. What is the right response?

choices.A: Give the headline accuracy figure
choices.B: Give the measure tied to the decision they face, and state what it does not cover
choices.C: Explain that this cannot be reduced to a number
choices.D: Give the model's benchmark score

explanation: A useful metric matches the decision and is honest about its limits. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark (D) can mislead, and refusing (C) fails the sponsor

question: A ten-user pilot is about to expand to two thousand users. What should the architect raise first?

choices.A: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
choices.B: License cost
choices.C: Whether a larger model is needed
choices.D: The training rollout plan

explanation: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and surfacing those is the architect's contribution. Cost (B), model size (C), and training (D) follow from knowing what breaks

question: How should a model be chosen for a solution containing several distinct tasks?

choices.A: Match each task to the smallest model meeting its requirement, and evaluate the choices
choices.B: One model everywhere, for simplicity
choices.C: The largest model everywhere, for safety
choices.D: The newest model everywhere

explanation: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate on evidence. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit

question: How should the context window be treated in a production design?

choices.A: As capacity to fill as completely as possible
choices.B: As a budget allocated deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
choices.C: As a concern only for long documents
choices.D: As a setting to increase whenever quality drops

explanation: Context is scarce and its allocation drives quality, so it is designed. Filling it (A) dilutes, it matters beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix allocation

question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across dozens of repositories. What is most durable?

choices.A: A policy document circulated once
choices.B: A single training session
choices.C: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
choices.D: Requiring approval for every use

explanation: Conventions persist when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (D) adds friction without conveying practice

question: A client will not accept a solution whose behavior cannot be explained to their auditor. What does this constrain?

choices.A: The model family only
choices.B: The cost model
choices.C: The architecture, which must make decisions traceable and the controls inspectable
choices.D: The deployment region

explanation: Auditability is an architectural property covering tracing and inspectable controls. Model family (A), cost (B), and region (D) do not by themselves make behavior explicable

question: What is the main risk of building directly against a single cloud's model service with no abstraction?

choices.A: Moving later becomes expensive, because the coupling reaches into application code
choices.B: Higher token cost
choices.C: Lower accuracy
choices.D: Slower responses

explanation: Coupling determines the cost of change, which is the architectural concern. Cost (B), accuracy (C), and latency (D) are not consequences of the coupling itself

question: A solution must serve users in two regions with different data residency rules. What follows?

choices.A: One deployment in the cheaper region
choices.B: A single deployment with encryption in transit
choices.C: Whichever region has the lowest latency
choices.D: Separate deployments whose data stays within each region's boundary

explanation: Residency is satisfied by keeping the data within each boundary. A single deployment (A, B) moves data across it, and latency (C) does not address the rule

question: A requirement is stated as make it as accurate as possible. What should the architect do?

choices.A: Choose the largest model and optimise from there
choices.B: Establish the accuracy the use case actually needs and what an error costs
choices.C: Build the most complex design the budget allows
choices.D: Defer the question until after the pilot

explanation: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against or verified, so it must be made concrete. Defaulting to maximum capability (A, C) spends without a target, and deferring (D) leaves the design unanchored

question: Two components each work correctly but the system fails intermittently at their boundary. What does this suggest?

choices.A: One component needs a larger model
choices.B: The contract between them is underspecified, particularly for edge and error cases
choices.C: The system needs more components
choices.D: The failure is transient and can be retried

explanation: Boundary failures between correct components point at the contract. Capability (A) and more components (C) do not define the interface, and retrying (D) hides it

question: A design proposes storing every model interaction indefinitely. What should the architect raise?

choices.A: Nothing, retention is always safer
choices.B: That storage is expensive
choices.C: That it will slow the system
choices.D: Why the data is needed, for how long, and what obligations retention creates

explanation: Retention creates obligations and risk, so purpose and duration must justify it. Treating retention as free of risk (A) is the error, and cost (B) and speed (C) are minor by comparison

question: How should a solution handle the case where the model is confident and wrong?

choices.A: Design so that consequential outputs are verified against something independent of the model
choices.B: Trust the confidence signal
choices.C: Ask the model to double-check
choices.D: Use two models and take the agreement

explanation: Independence is what catches confident error. Confidence (B) is not evidence, self-checking (C) is not independent, and two models can agree and both be wrong (D)

question: An evaluation shows 94% accuracy. What else must be known before this is actionable?

choices.A: The model version only
choices.B: The token cost of the evaluation
choices.C: What the 6% look like, and what each failure costs
choices.D: How long the evaluation took

explanation: A headline rate is only meaningful alongside the shape and cost of the failures. Version (A), cost (B), and duration (D) do not describe the risk

question: What should happen when a model version is updated beneath a production solution?

choices.A: Nothing, versions are compatible
choices.B: Increase monitoring for a week
choices.C: Roll back automatically if complaints rise
choices.D: Re-run the evaluation suite before the change reaches production traffic

explanation: A change to the thing that determines behavior invalidates prior measurement. Assuming compatibility (A) is unsafe, and monitoring (B) or reacting to complaints (C) detects after users are affected

question: A stakeholder asks why the solution cannot simply be fully automated. What is the most useful answer?

choices.A: That the technology is not ready
choices.B: That automation is always risky
choices.C: Which specific decisions carry accountability or are unverifiable, and what automating them would risk
choices.D: That the budget does not allow it

explanation: A specific, reasoned boundary is actionable and can be revisited. Generic claims about readiness (A) or risk (B) are not, and budget (D) is not the reason

question: What should be handed over with a solution so it survives its first year?

choices.A: The source code
choices.B: The evaluation suite, the criteria, the owner, and the routine for re-checking
choices.C: A recorded demonstration
choices.D: A list of prompts used

explanation: Continuity depends on being able to measure and maintain, with someone responsible. Code (A), a demonstration (C), and prompts (D) are artefacts without the means to verify them

question: A team reports the solution has become worse, but nothing was deployed. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.A: The inputs or the surrounding usage changed
choices.B: The model degraded on its own
choices.C: The prompts wore out
choices.D: The evaluation was wrong originally

explanation: Behavior changes with what is fed to it, and distribution drift is the usual cause. Models do not degrade unprompted (B), prompts do not wear out (C), and the original evaluation is not the first suspect (D)

question: How should prompts that determine production behavior be managed?

choices.A: Versioned, owned, reviewed, and evaluated on change, like code
choices.B: Edited in place when someone notices a problem
choices.C: Kept in a shared document for easy editing
choices.D: Frozen after launch

explanation: Anything that determines production behavior needs the lifecycle of code. Ad hoc edits (B) and open documents (C) invite unreviewed change, and freezing (D) blocks improvement

question: An organization asks how to measure whether Claude Code is worth the license cost. What should be measured?

choices.A: Number of tool invocations
choices.B: Change in the delivery outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
choices.C: Number of users onboarded
choices.D: Hours spent in the tool

explanation: Value is the outcome moved, not the activity generated. Invocations (A), onboarding (C), and time in tool (D) measure usage rather than benefit

question: What most often blocks a team from getting good results from Claude Code on an existing codebase?

choices.A: The size of the repository
choices.B: The programming language
choices.C: The absence of committed context describing the conventions and structure
choices.D: The number of contributors

explanation: Missing project context is the usual cause, and it is the one the team can fix. Size (A), language (B), and contributor count (D) do not by themselves prevent good results

question:
A legal-tech startup builds a contract assistant. The assistant answers questions about 40,000 vendor contracts. Users ask questions like "What is the termination notice period in contract ACME-2024-118?". Users expect the exact clause quoted. The team designs the RAG pipeline. The team must choose a chunking strategy.

Constraint: answers must cite the exact clause. Small errors in clause text are unacceptable to the legal team.

Which chunking strategy best satisfies the constraint?

choices.A: Split each contract into 2,000-token chunks with no overlap, to keep each clause in rich surrounding context.
choices.B: Split each contract into 400 to 600-token chunks with 10 percent overlap, and attach contract ID plus section heading as metadata on every chunk.
choices.C: Embed each full contract as a single vector and retrieve the whole contract, letting the model find the clause.
choices.D: Chunk by fixed 100-token windows with no overlap or metadata, to maximize retrieval precision.

explanation:
Why B is correct: The constraint is exact clause citation. Small chunks raise retrieval precision. This ensures the cited clause is actually returned. Overlap prevents clauses split across boundaries from being lost. Metadata (contract ID, section) lets the system filter and cite correctly.
A is wrong. 2,000-token chunks dilute precision. The retriever returns long passages. The model may quote the wrong clause from the same chunk.
C is wrong. A whole contract far exceeds useful retrieval granularity. The model cannot reliably locate one clause in 40,000 embedded documents.
D is wrong. 100-token windows with no overlap will slice clauses in half. Without metadata, the system cannot attribute a quote to the right contract.

question:
A sales team wants a Claude agent that can look up accounts and update opportunities in their CRM. The CRM exposes a stable, well-documented REST API with six endpoints. One engineer proposes building an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server; another proposes calling the REST API directly through function calling.

Constraint: ship in two weeks with the smallest maintenance surface. Only this one CRM is in scope.

Which integration approach should the architect choose?

choices.A: Call the CRM REST API directly through function calling, since there is one stable API and six endpoints.
choices.B: Build both an MCP server and direct REST tools, so the agent can choose at runtime.
choices.C: Use an agent-to-agent protocol so the CRM can negotiate with the Claude agent directly.
choices.D: Build an MCP server. MCP is the standard. Future tools will need MCP.

explanation:
Why A is correct: MCP pays off when there are many tools. It also pays off with dynamic discovery or shared servers across agents. With one stable API and a two-week deadline, direct function calling is simpler. It has less to maintain. This is exactly what the constraint asks for.
D is wrong. "MCP is the standard" is not a reason by itself. It adds a server to build, host, and secure. There is no capability gain here.
B is wrong. Maintaining two integration paths doubles the maintenance surface. This is the opposite of the constraint.
C is wrong. Agent-to-agent protocols connect agents to agents. They do not connect agents to a REST API. The CRM is not an agent.

question:
A support agent got 47 tools. Every internal API got its own function. After launch, the team sees slow responses. The team sees frequent wrong-tool calls. The model often picks a similar tool. The model picks the wrong tool.

Then the model retries.

Constraint: reduce wrong-tool calls without removing any capability the agent needs.

What is the best fix?

choices.A: Upgrade to a larger model so it can handle 47 tools more reliably.
choices.B: Add five more helper tools that pre-select the right tool for common cases.
choices.C: Group tools into fewer, well-named functions (or namespaced MCP servers) so the agent sees a small set of distinct choices, with details revealed on demand.
choices.D: Raise the temperature so the agent explores different tools more creatively.

explanation:
Why C is correct: This is tool bloat. A flat list of 47 similar tools makes selection a guessing game. Grouping into a small set of distinct, well-named entry points cuts wrong-tool calls. It also keeps every capability reachable. This is progressive disclosure of the rest.
A is wrong. A larger model costs more. It also adds latency. It treats the symptom (bad selection) instead of the cause (47 indistinguishable options).
B is wrong. Adding tools makes the bloat worse. It does not make it better.
D is wrong. Higher temperature increases randomness. This increases wrong-tool calls.

question:
An internal Claude agent reads and files expense reports through the finance API. It authenticates with a single shared service token that has full read and write access to every employee's expenses. A security review flags this before launch.

Constraint: the agent must act only within the requesting employee's own permissions. No shared privileged credential.

Which auth design resolves the finding?

choices.A: Remove authentication entirely and rely on the office VPN for access control.
choices.B: Keep the shared token but rotate it weekly.
choices.C: Give the agent one token per employee, all with full admin scope, stored in the agent's config file.
choices.D: Use OAuth 2.0 delegated tokens: each request carries the requesting user's own token, scoped to least privilege.

explanation:
Why D is correct: OAuth delegated tokens make the agent act as the user. The agent has only that user's permissions. This satisfies the least privilege principle. This removes the shared privileged credential.
B is wrong. Rotation does not change the blast radius. One leaked token still reaches everyone's expenses.
C is wrong. Per-employee admin tokens are still over-privileged. Storing them in a config file creates a new secret-sprawl problem.
A is wrong. The VPN proves network location. It does not prove user identity or authorization. Any user on the VPN can reach anyone's expenses.

question:
A chat triage agent classifies incoming support tickets. The current design uses a large model with long chain-of-thought reasoning: accuracy is 93 percent, but p95 latency is 6 seconds. The product requirement is p95 latency under 2 seconds with accuracy at or above 90 percent. Ticket volume is 300,000 per month.

Constraint: p95 under 2 seconds AND accuracy at or above 90 percent. Both must hold at 300K tickets per month.

Which design best meets both bars?

choices.A: Route with a fast model first; escalate to the large model only when the fast model's confidence is low. Verify the mix on a labeled eval set.
choices.B: Cache every ticket classification so repeat tickets never hit the model.
choices.C: Switch everything to the smallest, fastest model and accept whatever accuracy results.
choices.D: Keep the large model but cut the output token limit in half to reduce latency.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Tiered routing gets most tickets under the latency bar. A fast model runs first. The system escalates tickets with low confidence. A large model protects the accuracy bar on hard cases. The eval-set check proves both bars hold before launch. This meets the constraint.
C is wrong. It guarantees the latency bar. It abandons the accuracy bar. "Accept whatever accuracy" violates the stated 90 percent floor.
D is wrong. Cutting output tokens does not reliably cut 6 seconds to under 2 seconds. It risks truncating the reasoning. The 93 percent accuracy depends on this reasoning.
B is wrong. Support tickets are mostly unique. Cache hit rates will be near zero. This changes almost nothing.

question:
A production assistant handles 2 million requests per day across search, summarization, and tool calls. The team wants to detect quality drift, especially hallucinations, within one day of it starting. Today they only log the final user-facing text.

Constraint: detect hallucination drift within 24 hours at 2M requests per day, without storing every full prompt and completion (too expensive).

Which observability strategy fits?

choices.A: Emit structured traces (one span per tool call and model call with token counts and latency), sample a fraction of full transcripts, and run an automated faithfulness eval over the sample daily.
choices.B: Track only aggregate latency and token cost dashboards.
choices.C: Log only error responses and review them weekly.
choices.D: Store every prompt and completion in full, and hire reviewers to read them.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Structured traces give cheap, always-on coverage of behavior. Sampling keeps storage affordable at 2M requests per day. A daily automated faithfulness evaluation on the sample detects hallucination drift. This happens inside the 24-hour window.
C is wrong. Hallucinations rarely raise errors. Error logs miss them entirely. Weekly review misses the 24-hour window.
D is wrong. Full logging at 2M requests per day violates the cost constraint. Manual review cannot keep up.
B is wrong. Latency and cost dashboards say nothing about answer quality. Drift would be invisible.

question:
An IT helpdesk agent handles two query patterns. Pattern (1): "find the three most similar past incidents to this error message" (fuzzy, wording varies). Pattern (2): "what is the status of incident INC-48210" (exact lookup by ID). The team now chooses a retrieval strategy over the incident database.

Constraint: both query patterns must return correct results. Fuzzy queries need semantic matching; exact queries must never return a "similar but wrong" incident.

Which two approaches together satisfy the constraint? (Select two.)

choices.A: Use dense vector search for both patterns, trusting the embedding to rank INC-48210 first.
choices.B: Route the query first: detect an incident ID pattern and send it to exact lookup, otherwise use semantic search.
choices.C: Use dense vector (semantic) search for the fuzzy similar-incident queries.
choices.D: Use exact keyword matching on the full error text for the fuzzy similar-incident queries, so results stay deterministic.

explanation:
Why C, B is correct: The constraint has two halves. C supplies the correct mechanism for the fuzzy half. This is dense semantic search. B supplies the routing rule. Detect an incident ID and send it to exact lookup. Otherwise, use semantic search.

Together they cover both query patterns. They use the correct mechanism each time.
D is wrong. Exact keyword matching cannot handle the fuzzy half. If the wording of the error varies, keyword lookup misses similar incidents. Semantic search would find these incidents. Determinism is not worth missed matches.
A is wrong. Semantic search can return a similar-but-wrong incident for an ID query. The constraint explicitly forbids this.

question:
A team installs a community MCP server that gives their agent shell access. The server fetches its tool descriptions from a remote config file hosted by the server author. During testing, the agent suddenly tries to exfiltrate an API key after reading a tool description.

Constraint: the agent must be able to use third-party MCP servers without letting server content hijack its behavior.

What is the root cause, and the correct mitigation?

choices.A: Root cause: prompt injection through untrusted tool descriptions. Mitigation: treat MCP tool schemas as untrusted input, pin server versions, and sandbox or gate destructive tool calls behind confirmation.
choices.B: Root cause: the MCP protocol is insecure. Mitigation: stop using MCP and rewrite every tool by hand.
choices.C: Root cause: the API key was in the prompt. Mitigation: delete the key and continue.
choices.D: Root cause: the model is too small. Mitigation: upgrade the model.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Tool descriptions are model input. A malicious or compromised server can inject instructions through them. Pinning versions stops silent updates. Treating schemas as untrusted blocks the injection path. Sandboxing plus confirmation gates limit what a hijacked call can do.
D is wrong. Model size does not fix prompt injection. Larger models follow injected instructions just as well.
B is wrong. The protocol is not the flaw. Untrusted content is the flaw. Rewriting everything by hand removes MCP's value. It does not address the actual attack path.
C is wrong. Deleting the key after exfiltration does not stop the next attempt. It treats the symptom. It does not treat the injection.

question:
A code-migration agent must work across a 2-million-line monorepo. The first design loaded a summary of every file into context at session start. Sessions now exceed the context window before the agent does any useful work, and costs have tripled.

Constraint: the agent must navigate the full repo without loading it all upfront, and per-session token cost must return to the original budget.

Which context strategy fixes this?

choices.A: Switch to a model with a 1-million-token context window and keep loading all summaries.
choices.B: Use progressive discovery. Give the agent search tools. Give the agent file-reading tools. Give the agent an index of entry points. The agent pulls only the code it needs. The agent pulls code when it needs it.
choices.C: Compress all summaries with a smaller model before the session starts, then load the compressed version.
choices.D: Split the repo into 50 fixed partitions and run 50 agents, one per partition.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Progressive discovery replaces the monolithic upfront load with on-demand retrieval. The agent starts from entry points. It fetches only relevant files. This fits any repo size. It brings token cost back down. This is the textbook fix for monolithic-context failure.
A is wrong. A bigger window just delays the failure. It costs more per token. It does not change the wasteful load-everything pattern.
C is wrong. Compression loses the details migration work depends on. This includes exact APIs and edge cases. It still front-loads cost for code never touched.
D is wrong. 50 agents multiply cost and coordination overhead. Most partitions are irrelevant to any single migration task.

question:
A hospital uses a discharge-summary assistant. The assistant handles PHI. Legal requires patient data to stay in the hospital's AWS region. Legal requires no use of data for model training. Legal requires an audit of every access. The team considers the direct Anthropic API.

The team also considers Anthropic models on AWS Bedrock.

Constraint: data residency pinned to the hospital's approved AWS region, no training on PHI, full auditability. All three are legal requirements, not preferences.

Which deployment choice satisfies all three?

choices.A: Direct Anthropic API with zero data retention (ZDR) enabled, plus application-level audit logs.
choices.B: AWS Bedrock is in the hospital's region. It has a PHI-eligible configuration. It has a signed BAA. It sends inference logs to the hospital's audit store. No data leaves the region.
choices.C: Direct Anthropic API in the default configuration, since Anthropic never trains on API data by default.
choices.D: Self-host an open-weights model on hospital servers to avoid all third-party terms.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Bedrock keeps inference inside the chosen AWS region. This is residency. It offers HIPAA-eligible services with a BAA. This is the legal instrument auditors require. It lets the hospital own the audit logs. It is the only option that structurally satisfies all three legal requirements.
A is wrong. The direct API cannot pin processing and storage to a specific AWS region. Inference is global or US-only. Workspace storage is US-only. So, it cannot satisfy the residency requirement. ZDR plus a BAA would cover the other two requirements.

But residency is a hard legal bar here.
C is wrong. "Never trains by default" is a policy claim. It is not a regional control. It is not a contractual control. It fails residency. It fails auditability.
D is wrong. Self-hosting puts the whole compliance burden on the hospital. This includes hardening, patching, and auditing the model stack. It reduces model quality. It gives no legal gain over option B.

question:
A company builds a RAG system over a mixed corpus: long PDF policy documents, relational tables of product specs, and a codebase. One engineer proposes a single chunking rule (500-token windows) and one dense vector index for everything.

Constraint: retrieval quality must stay high across all three content types. A query like "which products support feature X and what does the policy say about refunds" must work.

Why will the single-strategy proposal fail, and what should replace it?

choices.A: It will not fail. Uniform chunking is the industry standard for mixed corpora.
choices.B: It will fail on cost. Replace it with a smaller embedding model.
choices.C:
It will fail. Different data shapes need different handling. Chunk PDFs by section. Index tables as structured rows with metadata filters. Chunk code by function. Use hybrid dense plus keyword search.

Do this over the combined index.
choices.D: It will fail on latency. Replace it with an in-memory cache of all embeddings.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Tables sliced into 500-token windows destroy row structure. Code sliced mid-function destroys meaning. Match the chunking to the data shape. This includes sections, rows, and functions. Use metadata filters and hybrid search. This keeps what each type needs for accurate retrieval.
B is wrong. The failure is retrieval quality. It is not embedding cost. A cheaper embedding of badly chunked text is still badly chunked.
D is wrong. Latency is not the problem. A cache does not repair broken chunk boundaries.
A is wrong. It denies the problem. Uniform chunking across prose, tables, and code is a known retrieval-quality trap.

question:
A travel company has two vendor-built agents: a booking agent (flights and hotels) and an expense agent (receipts and policy). They must cooperate: after booking, the booking agent hands trip details to the expense agent, which files the report. An architect must choose the integration mechanism between them.

Constraint: the two agents are separate systems from different vendors. They must exchange goals and status, not just raw data.

Which mechanism fits, and why?

choices.A: A shared REST API that both agents poll for updates.
choices.B: An agent-to-agent protocol, because the integration is agent to agent: they need to delegate tasks and report status, which is what agent-to-agent communication is for.
choices.C: Merge both agents into one agent with all tools, eliminating the integration.
choices.D: MCP, because MCP connects the booking agent's tools to the expense agent.

explanation:
Why B is correct: MCP connects agents to tools and data sources. It does not define how two autonomous agents delegate and coordinate. An agent-to-agent protocol is for this purpose. It handles task handoff, status updates, and negotiation between separate agents.
D is wrong. It misapplies MCP. MCP is agent-to-tool. It is not agent-to-agent.
A is wrong. Polling a REST API gives data exchange. It gives no task-delegation semantics. Each vendor would have to invent coordination.
C is wrong. The agents are separate vendor systems. Merging them is not technically feasible. Merging them is not contractually feasible.

question:
An accounting firm processes 20,000 vendor invoices each month. The steps are fixed. The steps are known. Extract fields. Validate totals against the PO. Flag mismatches.

Post to the ledger. The sequence does not change for any invoice.

Constraint: the process is fully deterministic in structure. Auditability of every step matters more than flexibility.

Which architectural pattern fits best?

choices.A: An augmented LLM with open tool access and no prescribed sequence.
choices.B: A multi-agent swarm where subagents negotiate who handles each invoice.
choices.C: A fully agentic system where the model plans its own steps per invoice.
choices.D: A workflow: fixed prompt chain with defined steps, validation gates, and logging at each stage.

explanation:
Why D is correct: The steps are known upfront. The steps never change. A workflow is the most reliable choice. It is also the most auditable choice. It removes the nondeterminism that the constraint does not want.
C is wrong. Agentic planning adds nondeterminism. It adds cost to a process. The steps of this process are already known. Flexibility is not necessary here.
A is wrong. Open tool access without a prescribed sequence makes auditing harder. It invites skipped validation steps.
B is wrong. A negotiating swarm is massive overengineering. This is for identical invoices with fixed steps.

question:
A CFO decides whether to fund a Claude-based contract review assistant. The vendor talks about "AI transformation." The vendor talks about "delighting users." The CFO asks for the business case in her language.

Constraint: The case must show measurable business value. It must not show technology enthusiasm.

How should the architect frame the value?

choices.A: Map the solution to value pillars with numbers: hours saved per contract, cost per review before and after, error-rate reduction, and payback period.
choices.B: Promise full transformation of the legal department within one quarter.
choices.C: Focus on the elegant multi-agent architecture under the hood.
choices.D: Emphasize that the system uses the most advanced model available.

explanation:
Why A is correct: The value pillars are efficiency, cost, productivity, and performance. The CFO's language is numbers. This includes hours, cost per unit, error rates, and payback. A translates the solution into these terms.
D is wrong. Model choice is an implementation detail. It is not business value.
B is wrong. An unmeasurable transformation promise is the hype. The CFO screens out this hype.
C is wrong. Architecture elegance does not appear on any value pillar.

question:
A market-research team wants a 30-page industry report generated from 200 source documents. A single prompt ("write the report") produces shallow, repetitive output that misses key sources.

Constraint: the report must synthesize all 200 sources with depth in each section.

Which decomposition approach fixes the shallow output?

choices.A: Reduce the source set to 20 documents so one prompt can handle it.
choices.B: Use a larger context window and repeat the same single prompt.
choices.C: Decompose: a planner outlines sections, researcher subagents gather evidence per section in parallel, then a synthesizer writes the full report from the gathered evidence.
choices.D: Ask the model to write the report one page at a time with no plan.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Decomposition matches the work to the model's strengths. First, plan the structure. Then, gather evidence for each section in parallel. After that, synthesize the information. Each step has a manageable context. This avoids one impossible large prompt.
B is wrong because a bigger window does not fix the lack of structure. The model still skims. It does not go deep.
D is wrong because writing page-by-page without a plan produces incoherent reports. The reports drift from the outline.
A is wrong because it discards 90 percent of the sources. This violates the synthesis constraint.

question:
A competitive-intelligence system uses one orchestrator and six researcher subagents covering pricing, product, hiring, patents, news, and social. Early tests show subagents overwriting each other's findings and two agents researching the same competitor twice.

Constraint: each finding recorded once, no duplicated research effort, and the orchestrator can see everything.

Which orchestration design resolves this?

choices.A: Run the six researchers sequentially so they cannot collide.
choices.B: Give every subagent its own private memory and merge by concatenating outputs.
choices.C: Let subagents coordinate peer-to-peer with a shared chat channel.
choices.D: Orchestrator assigns non-overlapping scopes, all findings go to a shared structured store with unique keys, and the orchestrator merges at the end.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Non-overlapping scopes remove duplicated effort. A shared keyed store prevents overwrites. Each finding has one key. The orchestrator keeps full visibility for the merge. All three parts of the constraint are met.
C is wrong. Peer-to-peer chat is not structured. Agents still collide. The orchestrator loses visibility into side conversations.
A is wrong because sequential execution fixes collisions. It does this by destroying parallelism. Six researchers take six times longer.
B is wrong because private memories plus concatenation duplicates effort. It produces conflicting merged output. There is no deduplication.

question:
A support team deploys an answer bot and adds a thumbs up / thumbs down button on every answer. After three months they have 40,000 ratings but answer quality has not improved. The ratings sit in a database nobody queries.

Constraint: user feedback must actually drive quality improvement, on a repeating cadence.

What is not present? What completes the process?

choices.A: More ratings. Add a popup asking every user to rate.
choices.B: This is a feedback loop. Sample low-rated answers each week. Add the failures to the eval set. Review prompt or retrieval fixes against the eval set. Ship what makes the score better.
choices.C: A bigger model, since ratings show the current one is weak.
choices.D: Delete the rating button; it creates noise without value.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Feedback makes quality better only when it goes somewhere. Failures become evaluation cases. You test fixes against the evaluation set. The loop repeats on a schedule. B builds the full input, processing, output, and feedback system. The constraint asks for this.
A is wrong because the problem is not rating volume. 40,000 unused ratings prove more data without a loop changes nothing.
C is wrong because the ratings do not diagnose the model as the cause. The failures can be retrieval or prompt issues. A bigger model would share these issues.
D is wrong because it destroys the signal. It does not use the signal.

question:
A team builds a code-review bot. It runs the linter. It runs the test suite. It reads the diff. It posts review comments. The sequence is always the same.

Writing the comments is the only open-ended part. One architect calls it "agentic." Another calls it "a workflow with tools."

Constraint: choose the pattern honestly so the team designs the right controls (and does not overbuild).

Which pattern is this, and why does the label matter?

choices.A:
This is an Augmented LLM. It is a workflow with tools. The path is fixed. The model fills in one open-ended step. The label is important. A fixed path needs validation gates.

It does not need agent loop controls.
choices.B: Fully manual, because a human must approve every comment.
choices.C: Multi-agent, because linting, testing, and commenting are three jobs.
choices.D: Agentic, because it uses tools. Agentic systems need loop limits and escalation controls.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Tool use alone does not make a system agentic. Who decides the steps is important. Here the steps are fixed. So, it is an augmented LLM. It is a tool-using workflow. The label controls the system.
Truly agentic loops need iteration limits and stop conditions.
D is wrong because it mislabels the system. Applying agent loop controls to a fixed pipeline adds complexity. It does this without benefit.
B is wrong because human approval of every comment defeats the automation goal. The design does not require this.
C is wrong because three sequential steps do not make three agents. Splitting them adds orchestration overhead. There is no gain.

question:
A trading desk wants a Claude assistant for pre-trade research. The desk's SLA: 99.9 percent uptime, p95 response under 3 seconds, including during market-open spikes when request volume jumps 10x.

Constraint: the SLA must hold during 10x spikes. A slow or down assistant during market open is worse than no assistant.

Which design best protects the SLA?

choices.A: Use the largest model for best answer quality and accept slower spikes.
choices.B: Disable the assistant during market open to protect the SLA.
choices.C: Provision for average load and add a queue; users wait during spikes.
choices.D: Design for peak with autoscaling. Add a defined degraded mode. Use cached or short answers. Show a clear banner when the full pipeline cannot meet 3 seconds. The SLA states degraded-mode behavior clearly.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Autoscaling handles the 10x spike. The explicit degraded mode means the SLA is honest. It states what happens under extreme load. It does not silently break. Stating degraded behavior in the SLA makes it a real SLA. It is not just a hope.
C is wrong because queuing during market open directly violates the 3-second p95 requirement.
A is wrong because it prioritizes quality over the stated SLA. The constraint ranks the latency bar above model size.
B is wrong because disabling the system at peak need is an admission. It means the design failed the SLA.

question:
An insurer designs a claims pipeline: intake (classify claim type), processing (validate against policy, estimate payout), output (draft decision letter), feedback (adjuster corrections flow back into the eval set). The architect must present the end-to-end design.

Constraint: every stage must be observable, and failures at any stage must be routable to a human without losing the claim.

Which design element is most critical to satisfying the constraint?

choices.A: Making the pipeline fully autonomous with no human queues, to maximize throughput.
choices.B: Combining intake and processing into one giant prompt to reduce handoff errors.
choices.C: Using the same model for all four stages to keep behavior consistent.
choices.D: Stage boundaries with structured handoffs: each stage emits a typed result plus confidence. Route low-confidence or failed results to a human queue. Attach the full stage history to each routed result. Log every handoff.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Structured handoffs with confidence scores make each stage observable. The human queue with full history satisfies the routability requirement. It does not lose claims. Logging every handoff gives the audit trail. It is the only option built around the constraint.
C is wrong. Model uniformity does not create observability or human routing. It is an implementation convenience.
A is wrong. It directly violates the human-routing half of the constraint.
B is wrong. Merging stages destroys per-stage observability. It makes failures harder to localize.

question:
A localization team must translate 5,000 product documents (each 20 to 80 pages) into 12 languages. Quality must be consistent across languages, terminology must match the company glossary, and the job must finish in 30 days.

Constraint: glossary-consistent terminology across all 12 languages, 30-day deadline, no quality drift between early and late documents.

Which orchestration strategy best meets all three?

choices.A: One agent translating documents sequentially in all 12 languages.
choices.B: Split documents into sections. Translate sections at the same time for each language. Inject the glossary into every prompt. A hierarchical merge step checks cross-section consistency. Then finalize each document.
choices.C: Twelve separate agents, one per language, each working independently with no shared glossary.
choices.D: Machine-translate everything first, then have one agent proofread all 5,000 documents.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Parallel fan-out meets the 30-day deadline. Glossary injection in every prompt enforces terminology consistency. The hierarchical merge catches the cross-section drift that parallel work introduces. Each constraint maps to one design element.
A is wrong. Sequential translation of 5,000 documents times 12 languages cannot fit 30 days.
C is wrong. Independent agents with no shared glossary guarantee terminology drift across languages.
D is wrong. One proofreading agent over 5,000 documents reintroduces the sequential bottleneck. The deadline fails.

question:
A CIO has budget for one AI initiative. Proposal X: automate invoice data entry (saves 4,000 staff-hours per year, measurable in 3 months, low risk). Proposal Y: an AI product copilot for customers (could open a new revenue line, 12-month horizon, high uncertainty). The company's stated strategy this year is cost discipline.

Constraint: the pick must align with the stated strategy (cost discipline) and be defensible with measurable value.

Which two statements best guide the decision? (Select two.)

choices.A: Fund both at half budget to keep options open.
choices.B: Choose X: it maps to the efficiency and cost pillars, matches the cost-discipline strategy, and its value is measurable within one quarter.
choices.C: Choose Y: transformation projects always beat efficiency projects in the long run.
choices.D: Defer the decision until both proposals have quantified value, cost, risk, and time-to-value estimates.

explanation:
Why B, D is correct: B and D work as a pair. B names the strategy-aligned pick. X maps to the efficiency and cost pillars. It is measurable within a quarter. This is what the constraint demands. D states the evidentiary standard that makes the pick defensible.
It requires quantified value, cost, risk, and time-to-value for both proposals. X already meets that standard. Y does not. This is exactly why X wins.
C is wrong. "Transformation always beats efficiency" is a slogan. It is not an analysis. It ignores the stated strategy. It ignores the measurability constraint.
A is wrong. Splitting the budget starves both proposals. It avoids the prioritization decision that the CIO needs.

question:
Give a research agent open-ended questions. An example is "what should our pricing strategy be?" The agent sometimes loops during testing. It calls the same search tools many times. It refines forever. It never makes the final memo. Each loop uses many tokens.
